planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in spring once frost danger has passed, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade; this Chinese holly fern forms a dense, slowly spreading clump of glossy, leathery fronds whose narrow pinnae curve distinctly to one side, giving the frond a sickle-like silhouette unlike the broader, straighter pinnae of the more common Cyrtomium fortunei and C. falcatum. It tolerates heavier shade and drier soil than most holly ferns once established, making it useful under dense evergreen canopies where little else holds foliage color through winter. Mulch the crown in the coldest end of its range and keep soil evenly moist through the first two growing seasons to encourage the rhizome to bulk up.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted rosettes in spring in a shallow, fast-draining mix over rock or hardscape in partial shade; resents soggy, compacted soil.

directions: Tuck divisions into crevices of rock gardens, tufa, or well-drained raised beds in partial to full shade; like the related resurrection plant, this East Asian spikemoss curls its wiry, scale-covered stems into a tight brown ball during drought and unfurls back to vivid green within hours of rain, making it a striking textural accent over stone or among dwarf conifers. It is markedly more cold-tolerant than most cultivated Selaginella species and can be grown outdoors well beyond the frost-free zones required by tropical spikemosses. Avoid rich, moisture-retentive soil, which encourages crown rot; a lean, gritty substrate that dries between waterings suits it best.

planting.note: Plant divisions after frost danger has passed in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade; protect from hard freezes.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade, sheltered from drying wind; this large Australian maidenhair spreads by a vigorous creeping rhizome, sending up widely spaced, broadly triangular fronds on wiry, near-black stipes that are considerably taller and coarser-textured than the familiar northern maidenhairs. Given a moist woodland setting it will colonize ground steadily, so site it where its running habit is welcome rather than among small, slow-growing companions. It makes an architectural large-scale groundcover beneath tree ferns and palms in warm, humid shade gardens but needs winter protection or container culture outside its frost-free range.

planting.note: Plant crowns or divisions in spring in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in part shade to full shade; spreads by stolons once established.

directions: Plant crowns in rich, humusy soil that stays evenly moist to wet, in part to full shade; this selection of the native ostrich fern produces a substantially larger vase of sterile fronds than the wild species, with fertile fronds that can reach roughly half again the typical size, making it a bold choice for large woodland plantings or streamside borders where scale matters. Give it the moistest, most fertile spot available — rich bottomland soil that floods seasonally suits it well — and allow room for the colony to spread by wiry black stolons over time. The young fiddleheads are a traditional spring vegetable but, as with the species, should only be eaten fully cooked and in moderation.
